Yeah this is an interesting issue. Both (all?) sides have merit, and they all have crap to them. The thing about email is a good point, that you can't use it to provide commercial services, and shouldn't regularly use it when a commonly available commercial service exists. On the other hand. if you're out in the jungle and need to keep in contact with other jungle outposts, the only commercial service is expensive satellite internet service. Also, regularly using amateur radio makes sure you keep your gear and skills in order instead of trying to drag them both up in an emergency situation when you can't effectively test it all and need it to work immediately.

The issue with protocols and encryption is a pickle too. There are a lot of services where the encryption simply can't be turned off or partially turned off while preserving secrets (like passwords and api keys). The rule isn't that things can't be encrypted, it's that the meaning of the communication can't be obfuscated. So there's nothing illegal about encrypting or hiding the specific content of an authentication exchange, so long as it's obviously an authentication exchange. But encrypting the body of every email sent is generally believed to be against the rule. So one is left to think about how an undocumented protocol might look compared to encryption. I think that would effectively obscure the meaning of the communication too.

And then there are problems like winlink by itself. It's dependent on the internet and lots of volunteer emergency services personnel like RACES and ARES use it extensively, often with little idea of how it works or what to do if it stops working. It's just "cool" and it can be connected to a radio.
Baofeng sells affordable handheld radios that can be programmed to ham radio frequencies using free software called CHIRP. It's a good entry point for anyone curious about ham radio.
